title: The edge rusher: rush the passer, keep contain (and why Travon Walker's ribs matter tonight)
html:
Why this lesson now: the Film Room mirror (football-brief, branch film-room) was checked this run. It still holds one logged game file (data/games/gmum7mktl1wy3.json, "Eagles at Bears, Week 3", no snaps logged) and no review files. The original football-film-room repository wasn't reachable (access denied: "not configured for this session"). So there's no new miss of yours to fix, and no snap of yours this connects to yet. This lesson adds a new position idea, building on Lesson 24 (count blockers vs. rushers) and Lesson 43 (the 3-technique). Tonight, Jacksonville's best edge rusher, Travon Walker, is questionable with a rib injury.

The big idea: the edge rusher lines up outside the offensive tackle. He's the defense's widest lineman.He has two jobs. On a pass, get to the quarterback. On a run or a scramble, keep the play from getting outside him. Coaches call that contain.Teams call him a defensive end (DE), an outside linebacker (OLB) or just "EDGE." Same spot, same jobs.

White squares are the offensive line (LT, LG, C, RG, RT); the white circle is the QB. Yellow circles are the defense: DL (defensive linemen) and EDGE (edge rushers). A, B and C match the steps below.

  1. A: the speed rush. At the snap, the edge rusher runs around the tackle in an arc toward the QB.The tackle has to slide back and out to meet him. If the rusher is faster, he gets the sack. If he's slower, the tackle pushes him past the QB.Good edge rushers mix in other moves: a bull rush (straight through the tackle) or a spin back inside.
  2. B: the pocket. The QB stands in a space the line builds around him, about 5 to 7 yards behind the center.The edge rushers squeeze it from the outside. The inside linemen (Lesson 43) push it from the front.When the pocket shrinks, the QB has to throw early, take the sack, or run.
  3. C: contain. On the other side, the edge rusher stays wide instead of diving inside.That shuts the QB's escape route. A QB who can't scramble has to stay in the pocket and throw.On a run toward him, the same job is called setting the edge: push the runner back inside to the linebackers (Lesson 44).
  4. Wednesday night: Toledo at Sacramento State. Toledo had 5 sacks and 12 tackles for loss.Sac State ran for 8 yards. Andrew Zock stripped the QB, and Nathaniel Chandler recovered (MAC). That's the pocket collapsing from both sides.Toledo won only 20-17, but its pass rush kept Sac State from ever taking over.
  5. More real examples. Houston's Will Anderson Jr. has 7.5 sacks this season, the reason the bet board likes Houston Sunday.Monday night, Chicago's Jeffery Simmons (an inside rusher, Lesson 43) had a sack in his first 10 snaps against Seattle.Inside rush plus edge rush is what turns a pocket into a trap.
  6. Tonight: Jaguars at Ravens. Jacksonville's Travon Walker is questionable (ribs). He was limited Tuesday and Wednesday (Yahoo).Baltimore starts undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano on a sore ankle. A QB with a bad ankle can't easily escape contain.If Walker plays, watch whether Baltimore keeps a tight end or running back in to block him. That's the "chip" from Lesson 39.

How to use it in your drill: before the snap, find the widest defensive player on each side. Is he standing up (an outside linebacker) or with a hand on the ground (a defensive end)? Count the blockers left in to protect (Lesson 24). If the offense keeps a tight end next to the tackle, they're worried about that edge, so lean pass with extra protection. After the play, ask: did the QB get flushed out of the pocket, and which way?

Why it matters for your bets: sacks kill drives. A drive with a sack scores far less often. So a healthy edge rush helps Unders and team-total Unders, like tonight's "Baltimore over 14.5" → NO. If Walker is ruled out, the brief's skip rule kicks in.

Real examples to watch (Pacific time): tonight, Jaguars at Ravens (5:15 p.m., Prime Video): watch number 44, Travon Walker, against Baltimore's left tackle. Sunday, Texans at Chargers (1:05 p.m., CBS): Will Anderson Jr. against a Chargers offense with 17 turnovers, most of them Justin Herbert's 10 interceptions.

Video: search YouTube for "edge rusher speed rush explained," "what is contain in football," and "Travon Walker sack highlights."

Practice it in Football Camp → (Station 2: The box)

quiz.q: Where does the edge rusher line up?
quiz.w: He's the widest defensive lineman, outside the tackle (EDGE in the diagram).

o: Stay outside so the QB or runner can't escape that way
quiz.w: Contain is the edge's job on runs and scrambles: keep the play inside, toward help (C in the diagram).

quiz.q: The offense keeps a tight end next to the left tackle before the snap. What's a good guess?
o: They're worried about that edge rusher
The QB will scramble that way
quiz.w: An extra blocker by the tackle (a chip, Lesson 39) means the offense fears that edge rusher. It's often a pass with extra protection.
